paper_title: Beyond the Happy Path: Generalizing Robot World Models from Simulated Failures

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.

Introduction Action-conditioned world models increasingly replace realworld rollouts for policy evaluation, data generation, and planning [9, 13, 43, 56]. Their value depends on predicting how different actions produce different outcomes. Manipulation is where this requirement is hardest to meet. grasp shifted by centimeter or closed too early does not simply fail. The object is pushed, tilted, or slips from the fingers. Yet their robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations [27, 39], so this branch of physics is rarely observed. We find that this happy-path bias is severe. On our simulated evaluation, five pretrained models from three families [13, 29, 37] achieve object-motion error at most 10.4% lower than static baseline that copies the first frame, and two are worse (Tab. 1). Their predictions keep objects near the initial pose even when the recorded object is pushed or rotated  (Fig. 4)  . Such predictions risk overrating the policies being evaluated [41, 51]. Recent work fine-tunes on failures obtained by perturbing or executing actions [28, 41, 47, 51]. These methods keep the original generative objective [51], supervise outcomes through progress or reward signals [41, 47], or learn failure dynamics without ground-truth failure videos [47]. Two limitations remain. First, contact dynamics occupy small fraction of each frame, so global reconstruction loss gives them little weight. Second, outcome-level signals indicate whether an interaction failed, not how the object moved. Simulation provides what real robot logs lack: failures can be produced at controlled offsets and timings, safely and at scale, each with exact object pose, contact, and surface geometry. We present WorldReforge, post-training framework that exploits this ground truth  (Fig. 1)  . The Reforge dataset contains 62k simulated trajectories over 96 objects, generated by perturbing successful reference grasps in translation, rotation, and closure timing. Trajectories link execution variations to observed outcomes, including contact formation and loss, pushing, tilting, slipping, and whether grasp is established and maintained. These labels support controlled training compositions. Reforge-Real provides 300 real failure trajectories for evaluation. WorldReforge adds two objectives to the generative loss. Interaction Alignment (IA) reconstructs object and contact regions with dedicated, area-normalized signal. Surface Correspondence (SC) requires intermediate backbone features to locate the same physical surface points across frames, supervised by simulator-projected trajectories. Neither adds inference-time parameters. Post-training on Reforge alone reduces object error by about quarter for Cosmos3 Nano and LingBot-VA, and IA and SC further lower or match every motion error across all three model families. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object ADE by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on objects unseen during post-training, and it predicts the divergence between two actions outcomes with 43.3% lower error. Trained only in simulation, it improves PSNR by 1.04 dB on DROID and 0.68 dB on real failure videos. Controlled data studies reveal division of labor. Adding failures in which the gripper closes without securing the object reduces object error on such contacts by 18.0%, while successful holding remains the best teacher for keeping grasped object stable. Our contributions are: diagnosis that pretrained action-conditioned world models barely outperform static predictor under failed contact, and the Reforge dataset, combining 62k simulated trajectories with dense physical ground truth, 300 real failure trajectories, and paired-action protocol for measuring response differences. WorldReforge, which converts simulator ground truth into interaction-region reconstruction and cross-frame surface correspondence objectives without inference-time cost. Evidence that simulated failures improve object and gripper prediction across model families, transfer to unseen objects and real-world video, and play role complementary to successful experience. 2. Related Work 2.1. Robot World Models Early action-conditioned video predictors model pixel motion [12]; Visual Foresight uses predictions for control [11], and SV2P models uncertain futures [1]. World Models learns compressed dynamics [16, 32, 33, 52], while PlaNet and DreamerV3 use latent rollouts for planning and policy learning [17, 18, 44]. Genie learns controllable latent actions from unlabeled video [3], RoboDreamer composes predictions from language primitives [62], and Diffusion Forcing combines causal generation with per-token noise levels [4]. UniSim learns interactive visual simulation [53]; Cosmos3 integrates multimodal generation and action tasks [37, 38]; DreamDojo transfers knowledge from human videos [13]; and LingBot-VA jointly models video and actions [29]. IRASim uses frame-level action conditioning [63], and Ctrl-World combines multi-view generation with pose-conditioned memory [15]. WorldReforge combines successful and failed experience for contact-driven object prediction. 2.2. Post-training for Physical Alignment Real-world interaction data and demonstration-based learning support robot manipulation [31, 34, 35, 39, 48, 49, 61]. RoboCasa and robosuite support simulated manipulation [36, 64], while Kubric provides synthetic videos with dense geometric annotations [14]. AHA constructs failure exam2 ples for detection and reasoning [10]. FACT and CureWM learn from executed failures [41, 51]; DreamTrue and HFWM use counterfactual or reward-guided training [28, 47]; WorldSync aligns generation with actions [5]. Feature alignment complements training: REPA aligns denoising features with pretrained visual representations [55], VideoREPA aligns spatiotemporal token relations [58], and PhysisForcing aligns feature trajectories and semantic relations [57]. ABot-PhysWorld uses decoupled discriminative feedback for preference optimization [6]. WorldReforge uses physical ground truth for local reconstruction and surface correspondence. 2.3. Evaluating Video and Interaction Physion evaluates physical prediction in controlled scenarios [2]; WorldOracle compares predictions with real executions [9]; WorldFailBench evaluates failure causes, stages, and boundaries [59]. Forecasting research motivates careful metric comparisons [24], and TAP-Vid provides pointtracking protocols [7]. RAFT estimates optical flow [46]; PIPs tracks individual points through occlusion [19]; TAPIR refines point trajectories [8]; and CoTracker jointly models tracks, with CoTracker3 scaling supervision through pseudolabeling [25, 26, 60]. VBench and VideoScore assess video quality across multiple dimensions [20, 23]. EWMBench evaluates scene, motion, and semantic quality [56], while WorldArena connects perception to data generation, policy evaluation, and planning [43]. Framewise appearance alone does not establish action-dependent physical accuracy. We separately evaluate object motion, gripper motion, and video quality, alongside paired-action response differences. 3. Method 3.1. Pretrained predictions remain near the initial pose, Reforge recovers the main motion trend, and WorldReforge follows the recorded direction, displacement, and final pose more closely. 5. Analysis We analyze how execution coverage, complementary successful and failed experience, action sensitivity, and physical supervision shape interaction prediction. 5.1. Execution Coverage Translation, rotation, and closure timing expose different aspects of objectgripper interaction. By varying their proportions in Tab. 4, we examine how these experiences contribute to object and gripper prediction, both within and across execution types. Each execution type is evaluated on the corresponding 200-video subset of Reforge-Eval. Object-response prediction. Combining translation and rotation gives the lowest object ADE under translation and rotation changes and across Reforge-Eval (7.25 pixels). It also achieves the highest PSNR on Reforge-Eval and both real domains. The rotation and closure recipe instead gives the lowest object ADE under closure changes, demonstrating the distinct value of different execution experiences. Complementary execution experience. Including closure alongside translation and rotation yields the lowest gripper ADE across all execution conditions, reaching 2.68 pixels overall. Together with the object-response results, this supports emphasizing translation and rotation while retaining closure experience for accurate gripper dynamics. These findings highlight the different contributions of execution types to object and gripper motion prediction. 5.2. (9) We first average the squared RGB residual across all pixels and future frames of each pair, then average across pairs. Object/gripper ADE and PSNR evaluate each predicted future against its corresponding recording. Table 6 shows that WorldReforge reduces response difference error by 43.3% relative to Pretrained and by 3.9% relative to Reforge on these pairs. Relative to Reforge, object ADE falls by 3.4% and gripper ADE by 2.9%, while PSNR increases by 0.09 dB. WorldReforge improves each branchs motion prediction and the difference between the two generated responses, linking trajectory accuracy to sensitivity to the action input. In Fig. 5, the marker slips during the grasp attempt in execution A, while execution successfully lifts it. WorldReforge reduces the residual around the object and contact region, more accurately reproducing the observed change between futures. 5.4. Ablation on Physical Supervision Table 7. Ablation on physical supervision for Cosmos3 Nano. IA emphasizes interaction-region reconstruction, while SC supervises cross-frame surface motion. All four variants are post-trained on 6.4k-segment subset of the Reforge dataset. Joint supervision lowers object ADE by 3.2% and gripper ADE by 6.3% relative to the stronger individual objective for each metric. It achieves the highest PSNR on Reforge-Eval and DROID and ties with IA on Reforge-Real. These gains highlight the complementarity of interaction-region reconstruction and cross-frame surface correspondence. Both objectives share the generative backbone without introducing additional inference-time parameters. 6. Conclusion WorldReforge strengthens action-conditioned world models through complementary interaction experience and physical supervision. The Reforge dataset connects execution variations to physical outcomes, while Interaction Alignment and Surface Correspondence focus learning on contact regions and cross-frame surface motion. This connects global video reconstruction with the dynamics of physical interaction. Our results show that failed contact enriches object-response prediction and successful holding supports state persistence. These complementary signals improve interaction prediction, real-world video reconstruction, and sensitivity to action inputs. Future work will extend this framework to longerhorizon manipulation and study how consequence prediction can support closed-loop robot control.

sections.content: Sec. describes dataset construction and real-world capture; Sec. gives training settings, evaluation protocols, and the visual-quality prompt; Sec. presents quantitative analyses; Sec. details paired-action evaluation; and Sec. provides multi-view qualitative results. Supplementary figures, tables, and equations use the prefix S. A. The Reforge Dataset A.1. Dataset Composition The Reforge dataset links variations in robot actions to observed physical consequences. It comprises 62,125 simulated trajectories and 300 real-world trajectories spanning 106 object assets. The simulated data support post-training and evaluation, while the separately collected Reforge-Real data assess prediction in real-world interactions. Tab. S1 summarizes both components and their failure-related trajectories. Tab. S1. Dataset composition. All 300 real-world trajectories in Reforge-Real are failure-related. Component Trajectories Assets Failure-related Simulation Reforge-Real Total 62,125 62,425 96 10 106 13,577 300 13,877 A.2. Reference Executions and Perturbations We construct successful reference executions using RoboLab [54] for robot simulation and cuRobo [45] for collisionaware motion planning. Perturbing end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper closure timing produces diverse contact processes and manipulation outcomes. Each execution records synchronized intervention commands, robot motion, and object states, linking action variations to their observed responses. Each intervention is specified by its reference frame, execution phase, direction, magnitude, and temporal profile. Translation primarily varies the horizontal end-effector position, and rotation primarily varies its orientation about the vertical axis; translations and rotations in other spatial directions are also included. Object properties, initial poses, and scene configurations define the physical context of each intervention. These contextual attributes are annotated separately from execution variations, allowing the dataset to describe how the same action variation produces different responses across objects and initial states. Tab. S2. Execution categories of simulated trajectories. Each trajectory has one primary execution category and may carry multiple physical outcome labels. Primary execution category Trajectories Translation Rotation Closure timing Unperturbed reference Total 51,964 5,720 4,356 85 62,125 A.3. Hierarchical Physical Annotations Output annotations describe interactions at three levels: contact events, object responses, and grasp outcomes. Contact formation and loss characterize robotobject contact; translation, rotation, tilt, and relative slip describe object motion; grasp outcomes indicate whether grasp is established and maintained during observation. These annotations are temporally aligned and may coexist: an object can rotate while remaining grasped, or move under contact without being lifted. Tab. S3. Physical annotations of simulated trajectories. Contact, motion, and grasp labels may overlap, so trajectory can contribute to multiple event categories. Contact detection combines target object finger contact flags with measured force magnitude above 0.05 N; contact is considered sustained when these conditions hold for three consecutive observations. Motion thresholds adapt to object scale. Let denote the shorter horizontal extent of the objects collision geometry at its initial orientation. The translation threshold is δx = clip(0.1s, 0.004, 0.012) m, (S1) threshold is arcsin(min(1, 2δx/s)), and the angular clamped to 1025. Motion events must exceed the threshold for three consecutive observations and coincide with 13 contact or motion continuing after contact loss. Pushing additionally requires support-state evidence that the object moves along supporting surface. Post-grasp slip denotes relative motion between an object and the gripper after the gripper has begun supporting it, with displacement threshold of clip(0.15s, 0.006, 0.020) m. Dropping denotes subsequent separation from the supporting gripper followed by downward motion. A.4. Successful Holding and Failed Contact Successful holding and failed contact provide complementary interaction experience. Holding captures state persistence after grasp establishment, whereas failed attempts reveal contact-driven object responses. Failed-contact segments are grouped into contracted contact and open contact according to the measured gripper state. The composition experiments use the normalized closure at the final frame of each segment: values above 0.25 indicate contracted contact, and the remaining values indicate open contact. This grouping characterizes the contact configuration within segment. A.5. Reforge-Real: Hardware and Data Capture Reforge-Real uses seven-degree-of-freedom Franka Panda arm with Franka Hand electric parallel-jaw gripper, teleoperated through SpaceMouse and the Deoxys OSC_POSE interface. Fig. S1 shows the capture setup and synchronized three-view observations; Tab. S4 lists the hardware and acquisition settings. Tab. S4. Reforge-Real hardware and acquisition settings. RGB frame rates are requested settings; control and state frequencies are approximate measurements. Component Configuration Franka Panda, 7 DoF Franka Hand, electric parallel-jaw gripper ZED-M, rectified left image Intel RealSense D435IF Intel RealSense D435 SpaceMouse; Deoxys OSC_POSE 1280 720, requested 15 FPS Robot arm Gripper Wrist RGB External RGB 1 External RGB 2 Teleoperation RGB capture Control commands Approximately 20 Hz Arm/gripper states Recorded streams Approximately 99 Hz/10 Hz RGB, robot states, control commands, timestamps wrist-mounted Stereolabs ZED-M and two fixed external cameras, an Intel RealSense D435IF and D435, observe each interaction. All three RGB streams are configured at 1280 720 and 15 FPS. Control commands, end-effector poses, joint and gripper states, and timestamps are recorded alongside the images. End-effector poses are expressed in the robot base frame. Control commands, arm states, and gripper states are recorded at approximately 20, 99, and 10 Hz, respectively. The collection comprises 30 trajectories for each of 10 everyday object categories, totaling 300 failure-related trajectories. Fruit, beverage containers, plush toys, and markers vary in shape and rigidity, providing diverse contact conditions. Observation and state streams retain both host and device timestamps. The three views shown in the figures are aligned by nearest-neighbor matching of host monotonic reception timestamps. Fig. S5 further illustrates the temporal evolution of real-world interactions. B. Experimental Settings B.1. Implementation Details Our experiments cover five backbones from the Cosmos3, DreamDojo, and LingBot-VA families [13, 29, 37]. Each model predicts 16 future frames conditioned on the initial observation and 16-step robot action sequence. Actions comprise end-effector translation, six-dimensional rotation representation, and gripper state. Each action component is normalized using training-data quantiles as 2(a q.01)/ max(q.99 q.01, 108) 1, where q.01 and q.99 denote the first and 99th percentiles. Training and optimization. We conduct post-training experiments on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs, using global batch size of 64, BF16 computation, and FP32 optimizer states. The VAE is frozen, while the generative backbone is updated. We use AdamW with ϵ = 108 and zero weight decay. The training seed is 62101. Cosmos3 and DreamDojo use (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.99) with gradient-clipping threshold of 1.0; LingBot-VA uses (0.9, 0.95) and 2.0, respectively. For Cosmos3 and DreamDojo, the learning rate warms up to 106 over 100 steps and then decays linearly. LingBot-VA warms up to 3 106 over 100 steps and maintains that rate thereafter. Data-composition experiments use the initial portion of the main training schedule. The added robot-action input columns in DreamDojo are initialized to zero and trained. In LingBot-VA, trainable action_embedder encodes input actions into features. Physical supervision. IA emphasizes reconstruction in interaction regions, while SC establishes cross-frame correspondences using visible physical surface points. SC performs soft matching directly on backbone features, without an additional projection head. Each segment uses at most 16 object points visible Fig. S1. The margin defines the neighborhood; no separate contact mask, occlusion filtering, or smoothing is used. Masks follow synchronized poses of the same object geometry. Supplementary Quantitative Analysis This section addresses three questions: which interaction responses benefit from physical supervision, how simulated experience transfers to real videos, and how these gains vary with backbone scale and training progress. Throughout the result tables, bold denotes the best result and underlining, where used, the second best within each metric and comparison group. C.1. Interaction Conditions Condition-wise comparisons clarify the role of physical supervision in execution variations, failed contact, and successful holding. Tab. S8 decomposes the main Cosmos3 Nano results into six conditions, evaluating object responses, gripper motion, and video quality separately. Compared with Reforge, WorldReforge achieves lower object and gripper ADE and higher PSNR in all six conditions, with object-ADE reductions ranging from 2.35% to 6.96%. The same physical-supervision objective improves both motion responses during failed contact and state persistence after successful grasping. C.2. Successful and Failed Real-World Interactions Prediction on real interactions reveals the transfer value of simulated experience. Tab. S9 compares reconstruction and visual quality across the three backbone families on DROIDs successful and failed interactions. For Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge improves PSNR over Pretrained by 0.92 and 1.34 dB on the failure and success groups, respectively, with physical supervision further improving PSNR and SSIM over Reforge. LingBot-VA shows the same trend. DreamDojo improves visible integrity, reaching pass rates of 98.57% and 96.67% on the two groups. Together, the reconstruction and visual-quality results demonstrate the transfer value of simulated experience: post-training on simulation helps predict both failed attempts and successful operations in the real world.
